Howdy from a Hytale Dev! For all of our Modders and Server Hosts, we wanted to let you know that today’s pre-release officially depreciates the Netty Network Transport, for it to be fully removed in Update 0.9. Here’s how it affects you:

Players: You don’t need to do anything, this update shouldn’t affect you unless you have a weird platform. If you run into any issues, please fill out a bug report!

Server Hosts: Check your launch scripts! There are a couple flags that could cause issues now, check out the migration guide at the end of this post for full documentation about the flags!

Plugin Authors: Everything Netty-Specific has been marked Deprecated, which means your plugin will still compile and run for the full 0.8 lifecycle, but you’ll see removal warnings. There are a couple major changes to packet handlers and priorities, as well as pipelines with no replacements. Check out the migration guide at the end of this for exactly what has changed.

Finally, some platforms may not have a Quiche native library yet. On those, the server currently falls back to Netty and logs an error. If you see any of these errors, please send in a bug report that includes your platform name and architecture, the more you can get us the better, so we can get you support before 0.9 releases!

A full migration guide can be found here, as well as some code snippets, and other information: pre-release.docs.hytale.com/…

Thank you all for working with us as we work to make the game better, and more reliable!

The ECS is just an implementation of a technique called "Arrays of Structs". The goal is to both have code locality to optimize CPU cache (avoid waiting for RAM) and dynamic code. en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AoS_an…

A game like Hytale could work without an ECS and probably be easier to author BUT it opens us up to native modding without any modloader. The ECS is simply a way to make both the data and the logic composable while also not hard-coupling them together.

That's the plan but it still comes with inherent cost due to supporting both architectures and if we don't want to duplicate code, we still have overhead.
It's doable but pretty labor intensive. We are looking at transitioning some systems earlier than others but it is very low level engine architecture to work on the threading model - especially when the client is already suffering from the server stealing resources in singleplayer.

We dont really have a concurrent playercount target as it heavily depends on the way you use the server and such metrics often end up overly academic with too many variables.
The main problem is the nature of realtime simulations. If you have many players in one spot with very few NPCs the count is different compared to many players into completely different parts of the world with thousands of NPCs and many chunks loaded. 
Its different again if you completely seperate the worlds through instances. Generally we want to have 100-250 player servers with vanilla exploration / adventure to be possible if you have the hardware. 
Right now the server still depends too much of single-core performance and we are not leveraging the concurrency capabilities of the ECS enough. We lack a scheduler in the ECS which is capable to parallelise work where it's possible.
Giving you a concrete example of a simulation example: 
(1) Imagine you have a solar system: Every body affects the other bodies, so you have to split the logic into a gravity calculation, force application and velocity application step. It's possible to parallelize.
(2) Imagine you have a collision system of multiple bodies colliding. Who bounces where? There needs to be a "communication" between the bodies - it's much harder to parallelise. 
This is the core of the problem - we need that scheduler that plans the work and we need every system to be looked at and optimized / rewritten to enable splitting work.
On top of all of this comes the fact we don't just have 32-core CPUs but also 4-core CPUs and some people even just 2-core where the overhead of parallelisation isn't even worth it and further tanks performance on already weak systems.
I think we will make progress but it will be snail's pace.

We'd prefer to not do that for moderation. I have not had any good experience with automated moderation and especially in technical stuff like bug reports, we'd probably see a lot of mistakes. We also have had some pretty negative experience with community moderation and I really don't want to end up with reddit / discord / twitch chat mods situation. Not sure because that would mean we have to moderate the bug reports and there is quite a few.. let's say "strongly worded" ones :'D

We aggregate all bug reports in a spatial database and prioritize them by cluster size. So if you report a bug that isn't in a major cluster or itself affecting a lot of people - we'd handle it later.. There are over 100,000 reports we sorted this way 🙃 On top of that we also manually review bugs but due to the size of the dataset we can't manually review every bug. So individual tracking wouldn't really represent how we look at it because it may be looked at as part of a cluster but individually it's just a datapoint in a bigger galaxy of bugs.
